title: Twelve months close
hook: two poets, twelve months each, one longing

segments.voice: Yesterday, he comes home: in the cold months the bride found the holy place within, let go of self, and in mercy the Beloved came.

Two and ten. That's how the last stanza of Guru Nanak's poem counts the months: not twelve, but be das, two and ten, the way someone might count on their fingers at the end of a long year. Once the Beloved has come home, the poem looks back over all of it. And the Guru Granth Sahib holds a second year like it, by Guru Arjan, in Raga Majh. Two poets, twelve months each.
screen: `TWO AND TEN.` → `NANAK LOOKS BACK OVER THE YEAR.` → `A SECOND YEAR, BY GURU ARJAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the end of Nanak's year, not word for word. The two and ten months, the seasons, the dates, the days are good. The hours, the moments, the instants are blessed, when the True One comes and the meeting happens with ease. Hold that beside the whole year. Spring was good, and she ached. The hot months were good, and she burned. The rains were good, and she lay awake. Nothing about the weather was wrong. What changed was the meeting, and once it came, every month looked different looking back, even the hard ones. Now set Guru Arjan's year beside it, which this path read in year two. His months are in Raga Majh, and they too move from Chet around to Phalgun, a bride separated and asking to be united. In his Chet, remembering the Lord brings joy. In his Asarh, the heat burns the ones who don't keep the Lord near. Two Gurus, two ragas, two voices, sharing the same bones: a calendar the farmer and the bride both know, a longing in every month, and an ending where time itself is blessed. That's what a Barah Maha does. It doesn't wait for one perfect season. It takes the ordinary year, every page of it, and lets each month carry the same love. Not one season is left out. That's today's line: every season longs.
screen: `TWO AND TEN MONTHS ARE GOOD.` · `THE MEETING CHANGES THE YEAR.` · `GURU ARJAN'S YEAR, IN MAJH.` · `SAME BONES: A YEAR OF LONGING.` · then, large: `EVERY SEASON LONGS.`

segments.voice: Bring back one season of your life that felt like waiting, a hard winter, a time when someone was missing, and let a few details return: the light, the smell, where you lived. Then bring back a season that felt like arriving, hold the two side by side, and notice the part of you that was longing all along. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath, with thanks for both.
Twelve months close. Guru Nanak's year ends by calling every month, day and moment good once the True One comes, and Guru Arjan's year in Majh shares the same longing. Today's word.
Your line: every season longs. Even the waiting months belong to the year. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Both Barah Mahas are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib; in some gurdwaras Guru Arjan's stanza for the new month is read on Sangrand, the first day of the month.

chat.says: Why does Nanak's poem end by calling every month good, even the painful ones?
options: Because once the True One comes, the meeting blesses every season, even the hard ones.
Because the poem says the painful months were punishments that finally ended.
Because the farmer's year ended with a good harvest after all.
chat.meaning: The closing stanza calls the two and ten months, the days and the moments good and blessed when the True One comes and the meeting happens.
